summary: Deep dive on throughput tuning for AtlasAI's LLM workloads. Covered continuous batching, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, batch_time_ms), token limits, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps to run benchmarks and share tuning docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE. Daniel, why don't you intro?
[00:06] Daniel Ortiz: Hey all, Daniel Ortiz, SE on the inference team. We'll talk through throughput tuning and some knobs you can try.
[00:12] Priya Rao: Thanks. We're really trying to get predictable throughput for our multi-tenant API. Main pain is tail latency spikes when we run batch jobs.
[00:20] Tom Gallagher: Yeah infra wise we have 4xA100s per node, connected with NVLink, and we do a mix of short chat prompts (~40 tokens) and long summarization calls up to 8k.
[00:31] Sara Kim: And we run inside a VPC with strict egress rules, so any cross-region fallbacks are problematic.
[00:38] Daniel Ortiz: Ok noted. Quick agenda: continuous batching basics, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and batch_time_ms, token limits and padding, KV cache and prefix caching, quantization, and then bench discussion.
[00:47] Priya Rao: sounds good.
[00:49] Maya Chen: Quick question on success criteria — what are you optimizing for, cost per token or p50 latency?
[00:55] Priya Rao: Primary is predictable p95 under 300ms for short prompts, but we'd like to keep overall cost < $0.002/token for high-volume endpoints.
[01:05] Daniel Ortiz: Good tradeoff. Continuous batching trades a bit of p50 for much better throughput and cost. The core knobs are max_num_seqs (controls multiplexing), batch_time_ms (how long scheduler waits for sequences), and max_tokens_per_batch.
[01:20] Tom Gallagher: We tried increasing batch size but saw higher tail latencies. We didn't tune max_num_seqs specifically.
[01:26] Daniel Ortiz: That matches. If max_num_seqs is too high, you can get head-of-line blocking — long sequences hold KV cache across the batch and increase latency for short ones.
[01:36] Sara Kim: KV cache — is that per-sequence or shared? We worry about memory blowouts with 8k context.
[01:42] Daniel Ortiz: It's per-sequence in the runtime, but the scheduler groups sequences so their KV caches live concurrently on GPU. For long contexts you want to limit max_num_seqs or enable prefix caching so repeated prompt prefixes are cached and reused. Prefix caching reduces work for repeated system messages.
[01:55] Priya Rao: prefix caching — we have many identical system prompts across tenants, that could help.
[02:00] Daniel Ortiz: Exactly. Also consider quantization; 4-bit quant gets you memory savings and better throughput but can change perf characteristics, sometimes increasing CPU post-processing.
[02:08] Tom Gallagher: Any gotchas with 4-bit quant and NVLink?
[02:12] Daniel Ortiz: Mostly model-specific; for some models operator fusion changes and you may see different kernel choices. We recommend A/B the quantized variant under your workload.
[02:20] [02:20] Maya Chen: Could you sketch a tuning plan?
[02:23] Daniel Ortiz: Sure. Phase 1: baseline single-request perf (no batching) to measure token TTF. Phase 2: enable continuous batching with conservative knobs: max_num_seqs=8, batch_time_ms=20, max_tokens_per_batch=2048. Measure p50/p95/p99 and GPU util. Phase 3: increase max_num_seqs to 16 then 32 while watching tail latency and memory. Phase 4: try prefix caching plus quantized model.
[02:44] Priya Rao: Why start at 8?
[02:46] Daniel Ortiz: It's a balance — small enough to avoid long seqs saturating memory, big enough to get multiplexing benefits on A100s. Also watch batch token padding; if your short prompts are padded to long sequences you'll lose gains.
[02:57] Tom Gallagher: Padding is big problem: short chat padded to 8k because we batch with long ones. Any mitigation?
[03:04] Daniel Ortiz: Two options: enforce route-level token limits (e.g., max_request_tokens=1024) or separate traffic by request size into different queues/pools. Redwood routing policies can send long requests to dedicated nodes.
[03:15] Priya Rao: Can we do that in our VPC/self-hosted?
[03:18] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports routing policies in the control plane; on-prem you run the agent and configure pools. There's some network egress config for cross-node telemetry but no forced egress to public internet.
[03:29] Sara Kim: On networking — we saw packet drops with busy NVLink during peak. Any opinion on intra-node sharding vs model sharding?
[03:35] Daniel Ortiz: If NVLink saturation is an issue, consider tensor-slicing strategies: data parallel plus expert model sharding to reduce cross-GPU comms. Also CPU pinned memory and larger micro-batches can amortize comms. We can share kernel selection notes for that.
[03:47] Tom Gallagher: Scheduler fairness — do we have knobs to avoid one tenant stealing batches?
[03:51] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, scheduler has fairness weight per tenant and per-route priority. There's also a hard cap on concurrent sequences per tenant to prevent noisy neighbors.
[03:59] Priya Rao: How does max_num_seqs differ from batch_size?
[04:02] Daniel Ortiz: batch_size is the number of sequences in a single GPU batch submit; max_num_seqs is an upper bound across the scheduler's multiplexing before a submit, including sequences that might be waiting for tokens. It's subtle: batch_size affects kernel launch size; max_num_seqs affects memory and multiplexing window.
[04:17] Maya Chen: Example: if you have a 4-GPU pod and batch_size=8, you submit 8 seqs per GPU; max_num_seqs=32 allows scheduler to aggregate across time to fill submits.
[04:27] Sara Kim: We noticed stall when one seq does long sampling top-k/k sampling — how to avoid that?
[04:31] Daniel Ortiz: sampling loops can be preemptive in newer runtime builds; you can set token_timeouts and per-step budget. Also consider greedy sampling for high-QPS endpoints.
[04:42] Priya Rao: Token limits — if a request exceeds token_max, do we drop or truncate?
[04:46] Daniel Ortiz: Runtime policy can either reject (400) or truncate. We recommend rejecting for predictable latency. For partial results, streaming helps.
[04:53] Tom Gallagher: On metrics — what to capture to evaluate a tuning run?
[04:57] Daniel Ortiz: p50/p95/p99 latency per route, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory headroom, batch composition (% long vs short), padding ratio, KV cache hit rate.
[05:08] Priya Rao: You mentioned batch_time_ms earlier — increasing it increases throughput but hurts latency right?
[05:12] Daniel Ortiz: Exactly, it's the scheduler's sleep window. Lower values favor latency (less wait) but reduce batching. There's also an adaptive mode where the runtime can expand the window under high util.
[05:22] Maya Chen: Any heuristics for mixed workloads?
[05:25] Daniel Ortiz: Separate short/long routes with routing policies, or use per-route max_num_seqs tuned to expected length. For mixed single route, try small max_num_seqs but bigger batch_time_ms so you only multiplex similar sizes.
[05:38] [05:38] Priya Rao: How about KV cache eviction strategies? We have repeated sessions where older users' contexts hang around.
[05:44] Daniel Ortiz: Eviction by LRU and a max_cache_bytes per tenant are typical. You can also checkpoint and drop caches for inactive sessions. There's an API to purge stale prefixes.
[05:54] Sara Kim: If we enable prefix caching, memory goes up, right?
[05:58] Daniel Ortiz: It can if you cache many distinct prefixes; prefer caching common system prompts only. Metrics will show KV cache hit/miss ratios.
[06:06] Tom Gallagher: Any notes on quantization making p99 worse? We've seen some regs where quantized model had higher tail.
[06:12] Daniel Ortiz: Possible — quant may change numeric stability and cause more sampling retries or different kernel paths. Also some fused ops are slower in quant path. That's why A/B testing is essential.
[06:22] Priya Rao: For our 8k workload, will quant reduce memory enough to increase max_num_seqs?
[06:27] Daniel Ortiz: Usually yes, 4-bit can cut memory ~2-2.5x depending on model. That translates to higher concurrent sequences, but test to ensure accuracy.
[06:36] [06:36] Maya Chen: Let's walk through an example config for your setup.
[06:39] Daniel Ortiz: Given 4xA100, start with: max_num_seqs=12, batch_time_ms=15, batch_size_per_gpu=8, max_tokens_per_batch=4096, per_tenant_seq_cap=64. Route long requests to dedicated pool with bigger memory and lower max_num_seqs.
[06:57] Tom Gallagher: What about headroom for sampling loops and KV cache?
[07:01] Daniel Ortiz: Leave 10-15% memory headroom to handle spikes. Monitor OOM events. If you hit OOM, reduce max_num_seqs or enable streaming generation with smaller step sizes.
[07:12] Priya Rao: Streaming — how does it affect throughput?
[07:16] Daniel Ortiz: Streaming increases small RPC overhead but lets you emit tokens earlier. For long-running gen it's helpful as it avoids large batched tail. For throughput you may lose a little but gain latency predictability.
[07:26] Sara Kim: Any role for CPU-side batching? We saw high host CPU during token decoding.
[07:31] Daniel Ortiz: Offload decoding to GPU where possible; batch decoding on CPU can be made more efficient with vectorized libs. Also ensure Python GIL isn't your bottleneck if you run many clients per host.
[07:42] Maya Chen: We should probably capture a tuning matrix and run a couple of tests. Daniel can you outline the experiments?
[07:47] Daniel Ortiz: Yes. Experiment A: baseline single-request and measure. B: continuous batching conservative knobs (max_num_seqs=8). C: increase max_num_seqs to 16 and 32. D: separate long/short traffic route. E: enable prefix caching and quantized model. Capture the metrics we discussed.
[08:04] Priya Rao: How long should each run be to be meaningful?
[08:07] Daniel Ortiz: At least 30 minutes per config under realistic traffic to capture p99 behavior. If you have synthetic traces, run longer to capture daily variance.
[08:15] Tom Gallagher: We're worried about noisy neighbors. Can we cap per-API key concurrency?
[08:19] Maya Chen: Yes — per-key concurrency caps are supported, plus rate limits. That combined with per-route caps prevents a single client from saturating the scheduler.
[08:29] Sara Kim: For on-prem, any special config for Kubernetes?
[08:32] Daniel Ortiz: Use GPU node labels for dedicated pools, set resource requests/limits carefully to avoid scheduler preemption, and use local SSD for KV cache snapshosts. Also tune kubelet eviction thresholds for GPU memory pressure.
[08:44] Priya Rao: Is there an automated tuning tool?
[08:46] Daniel Ortiz: Redwood Optimize has recommendations and an automated profiler that can suggest max_num_seqs and quantization candidates. We'll share the profiling guide.
[08:55] Maya Chen: Ok let's move to specific numbers from your production traces. Priya, did you upload the traces?
[09:00] Priya Rao: I attached a sample CSV to the calendar invite, but I'll put a bigger set in the shared folder after the call.
[09:06] Daniel Ortiz: Great. We'll run an initial benchmark against a mirrored dataset. For the benchmark, please confirm the following: 1) representative request mix, 2) token length distribution, 3) whether you want model A (open-llm-7b) quantized or full-precision.
[09:20] Priya Rao: We'll send that. We mostly use a Llama-derivative 13B variant, but we can test on an open 7B first.
[09:28] Tom Gallagher: Any config for NVLink tuning?
[09:30] Daniel Ortiz: Ensure NCCL is tuned for multi-GPU, set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the right interface, and tune NCCL tree if you have many nodes. Also check interconnect perf counters.
[09:41] [09:41] Maya Chen: Are there any security concerns with prefix caching? We cache user prompts, is that PII?
[09:46] Daniel Ortiz: Good question. Prefix caching should avoid storing sensitive PII; you can restrict caching to system prompts and non-PII prefixes. For audited customers, Redwood can disable prefix cache or tone down retention. KMS integration ensures keys for model artifacts, separate from data.
[09:59] Priya Rao: For SOC2 concerns, do you have an audit trail for evictions and cache hits?
[10:04] Maya Chen: Yes, Private deployments include audit logs and you can enable extended retention for cache events. We'll share security docs.
[10:12] Sara Kim: Any chance of regressing quality with quant + batching?
[10:16] Daniel Ortiz: There's a risk. That's why we tie quality monitors and evals to your prompt suite; Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions.
[10:24] Priya Rao: Good. For the benchmarks, can you also capture quality metrics (BLEU-ish or semantic sim) so we don't trade off accuracy?
[10:31] Daniel Ortiz: Absolutely. We'll run the eval set alongside perf runs.
[10:34] [10:34] Maya Chen: Quick recap before we close, and action items.
[10:37] Priya Rao: Recap — Plan: share tuning docs, run benchmarks with specified knobs, provide traces.
[10:43] Maya Chen: Action items: Maya send docs and scheduler knob checklist; Daniel run benchmarks and share raw metrics; Priya provide traces and model choice. Follow-up call week of May 19.
[10:53] Tom Gallagher: Sounds good. Anything else on licensing or Dedicated pool sizing?
[10:57] Maya Chen: We'll include recommended Dedicated pool sizes in the doc. If you want an SLA, that's a separate add-on.
[11:04] Priya Rao: Thanks everyone, that was really helpful.
[11:06] Daniel Ortiz: Thanks, we'll start on the benchmarks once we get traces.
[11:09] Maya Chen: Closing — we'll send notes and links. Bye.
[11:12] End of recording.
